9router API key / secret exfiltration via /api/settings/database without prior login AIActions on Objectives Medium
After forging a session cookie, the attacker reads stored provider API keys and auth tokens from 9router's /api/settings/database endpoint. This correlates access to the settings/secret endpoints against the source ever having performed a successful POST /api/auth/login — a forged-token holder never logs in, so absence of a login is the tell. Rationale: Targets the article's named exfiltration path /api/settings/database ("steal valuable API Key, Auth Token") and the operational fact that a forged cookie bypasses the login flow entirely — so a leftanti against successful POST /api/auth/login isolates forged sessions. Sigma/Datadog/Defender/Falcon empty: this is a multi-event correlation on web-tier logs, not a single-event or endpoint signal. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/9router/CVE-2026-49352/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jphh-m39h-6gwx
ATT&CKT1528 T1552.001 T1550.001
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin session where the login POST landed outside the lookback window or was logged by a different proxy node (login not observed for that src)
  • Automation / IaC that reads 9router settings using a long-lived valid cookie and never re-authenticates in-window
  • Shared NAT egress where one user logged in and another admin IP-shares the same source address
  • Health-check or config-backup jobs polling /api/settings
Suppression filter
// Exclude known automation egress IPs that legitimately read settings with a persistent session:
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("10.20.0.15", "10.20.0.16")   // replace with your config-management egress IPs
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full request sequence for the SrcIpAddr; confirm the auth_token cookie matches the forged shape from UC1 and that no successful /api/auth/login exists for it across all proxy nodes. Check HTTP status on /api/settings/database (200 = secrets returned). 2) CONTAIN: Rotate ALL provider API keys and auth tokens held by 9router immediately (treat as disclosed), set JWT_SECRET + restart, block the source IP. 3) HUNT: Check for password-change and shutdown API calls from the same source, and for outbound use of the stolen keys against upstream provider APIs (billing/usage spikes).

| where SrcIpAddr !in (LoggedIn)     // forged-token holder never authenticated

9router unauthenticated MCP / cli-tools route RCE via process spawn — CVE-2026-46339 AIExploitation Medium
The 9router middleware only guards 8 routes, leaving /api/mcp/* and /api/cli-tools/* (40+ routes, added in v0.4.30) with no authentication, allowing unauthenticated OS command execution as the 9router user. Detects both the inbound requests to those routes and the resulting node process spawning a shell/interpreter child on the host. Rationale: Uses the exact vulnerable route prefixes named in the CVE-2026-46339 write-up (/api/mcp/*, /api/cli-tools/*, unguarded since v0.4.30) for the web tier, and the RCE's on-host signature (the node process spawning a shell) for EDR. Corroborated via the GHSA-fhh6-4qxv-rpqj advisory and Endor Labs' analysis. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-fhh6-4qxv-rpqj • https://www.endorlabs.com/vulnerability/cve-2026-46339
ATT&CKT1190 T1059 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate authorized use of the 9router MCP stdio->SSE bridge invoking a local tool that spawns a helper process
  • node-based build tooling / npm scripts on a shared dev box spawning sh/bash (scope the EDR rule to the 9router server to remove this)
  • MCP plugin health-checks or self-tests that shell out
  • Monitoring agents that proxy /api/mcp/ readiness probes
Suppression filter
// EDR side: scope to the 9router install path once known, to strip generic node->shell dev noise:
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("9router", "node_modules\\9router")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Correlate the /api/mcp/ or /api/cli-tools/ request time against the node->shell spawn on the same host; inspect ProcessCommandLine / InitiatingProcessCommandLine for attacker commands (whoami, curl, base64, reverse-shell). Confirm 9router version is 0.4.30-0.4.36 (unpatched for CVE-2026-46339). 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the spawned process tree, upgrade 9router to >=0.4.45, and restrict /api/mcp/ + /api/cli-tools/ at the proxy/WAF. 3) HUNT: Sweep for persistence and outbound C2 from the node process (DeviceNetworkEvents / NetworkConnectIP4 with ContextImageFileName node), dropped files, and reuse of the same source IP against other exposed 9router hosts.

| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh","bash","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")

GravitLauncher LaunchServer secret read via unauth path traversal (ecdsa_id/legacySalt/LaunchServer.json) AIExploitation High
Hunts unauthenticated HTTP requests to the LaunchServer file server that reference the server's own secret files outside updatesDir (.keys/ecdsa_id, .keys/rsa_id, .keys/legacySalt, LaunchServer.json). A successful read of ecdsa_id hands the attacker the JWT signing key, yielding a full admin auth bypass, so any such request is high-fidelity regardless of traversal encoding. Rationale: Uses the exact secret filenames the advisory names as readable outside updatesDir (.keys/ecdsa_id, rsa_id, legacySalt, LaunchServer.json) — legitimate GravitLauncher clients only fetch update payloads under updatesDir and never reference these, so any hit is near-certainly exploitation of CVE-2026-54617. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5g75-477j-2c2f • https://advisories.gitlab.com/maven/pro.gravit.launcher/launchserver-api/CVE-2026-54617/
ATT&CKT1552.004 T1190 T1552.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Nuclei) running a CVE-2026-54617 template against the LaunchServer host
  • Internal red-team / pentest engagement replaying the PoC
  • An update artifact legitimately named LaunchServer.json placed inside updatesDir and requested by a client
  • Security researcher probing the public 9274 endpoint after the CVE disclosure
  • Backup/monitoring tooling misconfigured to fetch config files over the file-server port
Suppression filter
| where DeviceProduct != "VulnScanner" and SourceIP !in ("10.0.0.0")  // exclude the sanctioned scanner subnet / host once identified
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request line and HTTP status for the source IP — a 200/OK with a non-zero body means the secret bytes were actually served (compromise); a 404 means the safe leading-slash branch was hit. Note whether the target was ecdsa_id/legacySalt (auth bypass) or LaunchServer.json (DB creds). 2) Contain: firewall port 9274 to internal only or rebind LaunchServer to 127.0.0.1; treat the ECDSA signing key, legacySalt and DB credentials as compromised and rotate all three immediately, invalidating outstanding JWTs. 3) Hunt: from the same source IP look for follow-on `../../../../etc/passwd`-style reads, and pivot to authentication logs for anomalous admin-account token use or DB logins from new IPs after the read timestamp.

| where RequestURL has_any (LaunchServerSecrets)

LaunchServer path-traversal exploit signature: request-target without leading slash / %2e%2e on port 9274 AIExploitation High
Hunts the structural exploitation signature of CVE-2026-54617 — an HTTP request-target that does NOT begin with '/' (e.g. 'GET ../../.keys/ecdsa_id') or uses '%2e%2e' encoding, aimed at the default 0.0.0.0:9274 file-server bind. This catches depth-robust arbitrary-file reads (../../../../etc/passwd) that the secret-filename query would miss, since only the no-leading-slash form escapes updatesDir. Rationale: Keys on the advisory's unique root-cause signature: only a request-target lacking a leading slash (or %2e%2e-encoded) escapes updatesDir, while curl/browsers/normal clients always prepend '/'. Port 9274 is the article's default 0.0.0.0 bind; the Defender/Falcon clauses only give coarse public-inbound-to-9274 exposure because FDR/AH carry no HTTP URI. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5g75-477j-2c2f • https://advisories.gitlab.com/maven/pro.gravit.launcher/launchserver-api/CVE-2026-54617/
ATT&CKT1190 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerability scanner firing generic '../' and '%2e%2e' path-traversal payloads at the endpoint
  • Misbehaving HTTP client or crawler emitting a relative (non-absolute) request-target
  • Legitimate query-string parameter that happens to contain '../' being logged in RequestURL
  • Load-balancer / L4 health-check tooling hitting 9274 with non-standard request lines
  • Defender/Falcon exposure clause alone: any benign public connection to 9274 (this clause is exposure, not exploitation)
Suppression filter
| where not (RequestURL has "../" and RequestURL !startswith ".." and RequestURL !has "%2e%2e")  // keep only the no-leading-slash / encoded form, drop benign embedded ../ in query strings
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the request-target genuinely lacks a leading slash or uses %2e%2e (the exploit form) versus a normal '/..' that the server 404s; check the HTTP status and byte count to see if a file was served. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the L4 firewall and restrict 9274 to trusted management ranges or rebind to 127.0.0.1; a normalizing L7 proxy in front returns 400 for these — deploy or enforce one. 3) Hunt: enumerate every distinct traversal target from that IP (etc/passwd, .keys/*, LaunchServer.json) to gauge what was read, and if any secret was served, rotate the ECDSA key/legacySalt/DB creds and audit downstream JWT and DB activity.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where LocalPort == 9274
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize Connections = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by FirstSeen desc
CommonSecurityLog

fast-mcp-telegram traversal token in request URL (URL-auth middleware) CVE-2026-52830 AIExploitation High
Hunts the URL-auth variant of CVE-2026-52830 where the traversal token is carried in the request path/query rather than the Authorization header. Surfaces web access-log requests to a fast-mcp-telegram server whose URI contains '../fast-mcp-telegram/telegram', %2e%2e-encoded traversal, or a direct telegram.session reference. Rationale: Pivots on the URL field instead of the Authorization header (the article calls out both header auth and URL auth, and URL-encoded traversal 'if any route decodes path components'), using the same concrete CVE strings so it catches deployments that log full URIs but strip auth headers. Distinct log field and platform coverage (CIM Web/W3CIISLog) from the header UC. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-52830 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/fast-mcp-telegram/CVE-2026-52830/
ATT&CKT1190 T1078.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Generic path-traversal web scanners hitting every endpoint with '../' regardless of app
  • Legitimate URLs whose query string happens to contain %2e%2e from over-encoding
  • Authorized pentest replaying the URL-auth bypass
  • WAF appliance logging a request it already blocked (filter on non-2xx status)
Suppression filter
| where status < 300 AND NOT match(http_user_agent, "(?i)(nuclei|zap|burp|nmap|acunetix)")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the URI targeted a real fast-mcp-telegram route and resolved to the telegram.session file (token '../fast-mcp-telegram/telegram' or %2e%2e variant); check the response status to tell an accepted bypass (2xx) from a rejected probe. 2) Contain: block the source at the WAF, patch to fast-mcp-telegram >=0.19.1, and invalidate/rotate the default telegram.session and its Telegram login. 3) Hunt: correlate the SrcIpAddr to subsequent MCP tool invocations and to the Authorization-header UC; enumerate other traversal encodings (Windows separators, absolute paths, double-URL-encoding) and confirm no messages were sent from the default account during the exposure window.
ImWebSession

    or (Url has "fast-mcp-telegram" and Url has_any ("../","..\\","%2e%2e"))
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, HttpHostName, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

9router node process spawns 'sudo -S sh' (GHSA-g6g7-pvmx-m74p command-injection primitive) AIExploitation High
Hunts the OS command-injection primitive in 9router's /api/tunnel/tailscale-install route: the Node.js server (or the '9router' binary) spawning 'sudo -S sh', whose stdin is fed the attacker-controlled sudoPassword field as a shell command. A long-running web server spawning an interactive privileged shell is the article-specific tell of exploitation (or of the rarely-used legitimate Tailscale install). Rationale: Anchors on the exact spawn from the advisory's tailscale.js:304-341 — spawn("sudo", ["-S", "sh"]) with parent node/9router. This process shape is emitted on every invocation of the vulnerable route, so it catches both successful root RCE and the process even when sudo later rejects the payload. Corroborated by GitLab GLAD and vendor repo decolua/9router. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/9router/GHSA-g6g7-pvmx-m74p/ • https://github.com/decolua/9router/security • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-fhh6-4qxv-rpqj
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1548.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate operator installs Tailscale through the 9router dashboard's 'Install Tailscale' button (identical process chain)
  • Other Node automation tooling on the host that shells out via sudo -S to run privileged install scripts
  • A configuration-management agent written in Node (e.g. a custom deploy daemon) invoking sudo -S sh
  • Developer laptop where 9router is run interactively and Tailscale is genuinely being installed
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessId != prev(InitiatingProcessId)  // dedup per server session; correlate with an unauthenticated/external source IP on /api/tunnel/tailscale-install before escalating
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the ProcessCommandLine of the child 'sh' and its subsequent children on the same host/session — the injected sudoPassword becomes the first shell command (look for 'id', file writes to /tmp, curl|wget, reverse-shell one-liners, or a trailing '; exit 0'). Confirm the parent node process is the 9router server and check whether it runs as uid 0. 2) Contain: isolate the host/container; if it is a container running as root, stop it and rebuild from an image that adds a non-root USER; rotate any secrets reachable from the process. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP that hit /api/tunnel/tailscale-install (web/proxy logs), and search other 9router hosts for the same node->sudo -S sh chain and for the sibling node->curl tailscale.com/install.sh event. Upgrade all 9router instances to >=0.4.45.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "sudo"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_all ("-S", "sh")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node", "9router")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessId, ProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "sudo"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_all ("-S", "sh")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node", "9router")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: 9router Node Server Spawns Privileged Shell (sudo -S sh)
id: 6b8f2e1a-4d2c-4f7a-9b1e-1c9a7f3d0e21
status: experimental
description: Detects the OS command-injection primitive in 9router (GHSA-g6g7-pvmx-m74p) where the Node.js server spawns 'sudo -S sh' to run the request-supplied sudoPassword as a shell command.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g6g7-pvmx-m74p
  - https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/9router/GHSA-g6g7-pvmx-m74p/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/07
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1059.004
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1548.003
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '/sudo'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - '-S'
      - 'sh'
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/node'
      - '/9router'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate operator clicking 'Install Tailscale' in the 9router dashboard
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.name:sudo @process.command_line:(*"sudo -S sh"* OR *"/usr/bin/sudo -S sh"*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/sudo$/i ParentBaseFileName=/^(node|9router)$/i
| regex("-S\\s+sh", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=sudo Processes.process="*sudo*-S*sh*" Processes.parent_process_name IN (node,9router) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=sudo Processes.process="*sudo*-S*sh*" Processes.parent_process_name IN (node,9router) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
9router node process fetches tailscale.com/install.sh via curl (vulnerable route invoked) AIDelivery High
Hunts the download step of 9router's /api/tunnel/tailscale-install handler: the Node.js server spawning 'curl -fsSL https://tailscale.com/install.sh'. Per the advisory's impact table this outbound fetch fires on EVERY invocation of the unauthenticated route — including cases where sudo later rejects the payload and no RCE occurs — making it the most reliable host-side marker that the vulnerable endpoint was reached. Rationale: Uses the exact command from tailscale.js: spawn("curl", ["-fsSL", "https://tailscale.com/install.sh"]) with parent node/9router. Because the advisory confirms this fetch happens even in the non-root 'no RCE' case, it is a lower-severity but higher-recall companion to the sudo -S sh detection. Corroborated by GitLab GLAD and vendor repo. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/9router/GHSA-g6g7-pvmx-m74p/ • https://github.com/decolua/9router/security
ATT&CKT1190 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator legitimately installing Tailscale from the 9router dashboard
  • Admin manually running the official Tailscale install command from a shell that happens to have a node-named parent
  • CI pipeline step that provisions Tailscale on a build agent via curl | sh
  • Container entrypoint that installs Tailscale at startup
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent is the 9router/node server and check for a following node->sudo -S sh event on the same host within seconds; review web/proxy logs for a POST to /api/tunnel/tailscale-install and whether it carried auth cookies or came from an external IP. 2) Contain: if the source was unauthenticated/external, isolate the host/container and treat as active exploitation; block the source IP at the edge. 3) Hunt: sweep all 9router hosts for this curl chain and for the sudo -S sh primitive; verify version and upgrade to >=0.4.45, and ensure the container runs as a non-root USER.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "curl"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "tailscale.com/install.sh"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node", "9router")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "curl"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "tailscale.com/install.sh"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node", "9router")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName

Unauthenticated POST to 9router /api/tunnel/tailscale-install endpoint AIExploitation Medium
Hunts HTTP access-log evidence of the 9router RCE (GHSA-g6g7-pvmx-m74p): a POST to /api/tunnel/tailscale-install, the unauthenticated spawn-capable route that bypasses dashboardGuard. Valuable for Dockerised deployments without endpoint EDR, where the reverse-proxy / app HTTP log is the only visibility into the attack. Rationale: Anchors on the exact vulnerable route path and method from the advisory (POST /api/tunnel/tailscale-install). Web-log visibility is the fallback pivot for root-Docker deployments that lack endpoint EDR; the request path is unique enough that any external hit warrants triage. Corroborated by GitLab GLAD and the related fix (CVE-2026-46339) that gated /api/tunnel/* to loopback. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/9router/GHSA-g6g7-pvmx-m74p/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-fhh6-4qxv-rpqj

Mautic CVE-2026-9559 Zip-Slip: web-server writes .php into config/cache/media dirs AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the core exploit artifact of the Mautic 7 campaign-import path traversal (CVE-2026-9559): the ZIP extraction escapes its staging directory and the web-server/PHP-FPM process writes an attacker-controlled .php file into Mautic's config, cache, or media directories. Legitimate imports never drop PHP into these locations; a new .php there under the www/AppPool identity is the RCE primitive. Rationale: Uses the article's exact exploit mechanics: the campaign-import ZIP extraction (path traversal) causing the web-server user to write .php into 'critical internal configuration or cache components' plus Mautic's media upload tree. Writing-process = PHP/web server restricts to the vuln context; the cache-container regex exclusion strips the biggest legit source. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/mautic/mautic/security/advisories/GHSA-6r9h-4h75-7q4x • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2026-9559 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/mautic/core/CVE-2026-9559/ • https://securityonline.info/mautic-security-vulnerabilities-rce/
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Symfony/Mautic cache warmup (bin/console cache:clear or first request after deploy) compiling container .php into var/cache
  • Mautic upgrade or plugin install writing app/config/local.php or plugin PHP
  • Composer post-install scripts materializing PHP into vendor/config paths under the www user
  • Backup/rsync tooling restoring .php into a media staging directory
  • Deployment automation running as the web-server identity rewriting config PHP
Suppression filter
and not (FolderPath has "cache" and (FileName matches regex @"(?i)(Container|_Kernel|CacheWarm|ProxyManager|getCommand)" or FileName endswith ".php.meta")) and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "cache:clear" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "cache:warmup"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the flagged file and read its contents — legitimate Symfony cache is machine-generated array/class code; look instead for eval/assert/system/base64_decode/`$_GET`/`$_POST`/`passthru`. Note the InitiatingProcessAccountName and correlate to a Mautic import in the app audit log within +/-2 min. 2) Contain: quarantine/delete the dropped .php, take the Mautic app offline or revoke campaign:imports:create for all non-admin users, and confirm the host is on Mautic >= 7.1.2. 3) Hunt: search the same host for a web-server process spawning a shell (see companion UC), outbound connections from php-fpm/httpd, and any other .php written by the web user in the last 14d; review web access logs for POSTs to campaigns/import.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName endswith ".php"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-fpm","php-fpm8.1","php-fpm8.2","php-fpm8.3","php","php.exe","php-cgi.exe","httpd","httpd.exe","apache2","w3wp.exe")
| where FolderPath has_any ("config","cache","media")
| where not(FolderPath has "cache" and FileName matches regex @"(?i)(Container|_Kernel|CacheWarm)|\.php\.meta$")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".php"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","php","httpd","apache2","w3wp.exe")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("config","cache","media")
| where not(TargetFilePath has "cache" and TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)(Container|_Kernel|CacheWarm)")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Mautic web-server/PHP-FPM process spawns OS shell (CVE-2026-9559 RCE outcome) AIExploitation High
Hunts the RCE payoff of CVE-2026-9559: after the malicious PHP is written via the campaign-import path traversal, the Mautic web-server or PHP-FPM worker executes it and spawns an OS command interpreter (sh/bash/cmd/powershell) or recon binary under the web-server identity. Web servers almost never legitimately spawn interactive shells, making the parent=PHP/httpd child=shell pair high-fidelity. Rationale: Targets the article's stated impact — 'Remote Code Execution under the context of the web server user' — via the parent=PHP/web-server, child=interpreter pair that a Zip-Slip web shell produces. This is the distinct process-tree pivot (vs. the file-write UC) and rarely fires legitimately, so it warrants alerting tier. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/mautic/mautic/security/advisories/GHSA-6r9h-4h75-7q4x • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2026-9559 • https://securityonline.info/mautic-security-vulnerabilities-rce/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Mautic cron/console maintenance (php bin/console ...) shelling out to helper binaries
  • PHP thumbnail/media generation invoking convert/gs/curl for remote asset fetch
  • Monitoring or APM agents having PHP-FPM run whoami/id health probes
  • Deployment scripts executed as the web user that call bash/curl
  • Legitimate admin-installed Mautic plugins that shell out for external integrations
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("bin/console","cache:clear","cache:warmup","messenger:consume","mautic:")) and not (FileName in~ ("curl","curl.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("127.0.0.1","localhost"))

1) Triage: inspect ProcessCommandLine of the child (recon like whoami/id, reverse-shell one-liners, curl to an unknown host = malicious) and identify the parent PHP request; correlate to a .php recently written by the web user (companion UC) and to a campaigns/import POST in web logs. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the offending php-fpm worker chain, revoke campaign:imports:create for non-admins, and block any egress IP the shell contacted. 3) Hunt: enumerate all children of the web-server process over 14d, review outbound DNS/connections from php-fpm/httpd, check for new cron/systemd/webshell persistence, and confirm patch to Mautic 7.1.2 across the fleet.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-fpm","php-fpm8.1","php-fpm8.2","php-fpm8.3","php","php.exe","php-cgi.exe","httpd","httpd.exe","apache2","w3wp.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","pwsh.exe","whoami","whoami.exe","id","curl","curl.exe","wget","python3","perl")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256

Mautic Twig SSTI RCE: PHP/web process spawns OS shell (CVE-2026-9558) AIExploitation High
Hunts the post-exploitation observable of CVE-2026-9558 — a Mautic web-tier process (php-fpm, php-cgi, apache2/httpd/nginx worker, or w3wp) directly spawning an interactive shell or recon binary. In a healthy Mautic install the PHP runtime never forks /bin/sh or whoami; when it does, an uploaded Twig theme has broken the sandbox and reached OS-command execution. Rationale: Grounded in Mautic's confirmed PHP/Symfony/Twig stack (advisory + GitLab/NVD) — the vuln renders theme Twig without a sandbox, so successful exploitation manifests as the PHP runtime forking a shell, which never happens in a benign Mautic web request. Parent(php/apache/nginx/w3wp)->child(shell/recon) is the highest-fidelity RCE pivot available without article-supplied hashes. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/mautic/mautic/security/advisories/GHSA-9fx4-7cmj-47vg • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-9558 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/mautic/core/CVE-2026-9558/ • https://www.thehackerwire.com/mautic-critical-ssti-cve-2026-9558-allows-rce/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Mautic scheduled tasks (php bin/console mautic:segments:update / mautic:emails:send) spawning sh for symfony process helpers
  • Composer/deployment scripts run as the web user invoking shell hooks during an upgrade
  • PDF/preview generation plugins shelling out to wkhtmltopdf or imagemagick's convert
  • Admin using a web-based file manager or terminal plugin on the same PHP-FPM pool
  • Monitoring/backup agents that exec via the PHP-FPM worker (e.g. New Relic, healthcheck shellouts)
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildCmd has "bin/console" or ChildCmd has_any ("wkhtmltopdf","wkhtmltoimage","convert -","composer") or ParentCmd has "bin/console")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ChildCmd and ParentCmd — a legit Symfony console task references 'bin/console'; an attacker command runs whoami/id/curl to an external host or reads /etc/passwd or Mautic's app/config/local.php. Confirm the acting host runs Mautic and check its version against 7.1.2/6.0.9/5.2.11/4.4.20. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the child process tree, and revoke sessions/API tokens for any Mautic user holding core:themes:create; block outbound to any C2 seen in the child cmdline. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same DeviceName for UC2 (new .twig under themes/), review Mautic audit log for recent theme installs, and sweep for dropped web shells or cron persistence written by the PHP user.

Weaponized Twig theme written under Mautic themes/ by web process (CVE-2026-9558) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the delivery step of CVE-2026-9558 — the Mautic web tier (php-fpm/apache/nginx/w3wp) writing a .twig template into the themes/ directory, i.e. an uploaded/created theme landing on disk. Pairs with the RCE detection: a fresh web-written theme template followed by a PHP-spawned shell on the same host is the full SSTI chain. Rationale: Mautic docs confirm themes are self-contained dirs under themes/ holding *.html.twig files, installed by uploading a zip through the web UI — so the payload physically lands as a web-process-written .twig. Scoping the writer to the PHP/web runtime (not an admin's editor) separates exploit-driven writes from developer file edits and gives a clean pivot to correlate with the UC1 shell spawn. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/mautic/mautic/security/advisories/GHSA-9fx4-7cmj-47vg • https://docs.mautic.org/en/5.2/builders/creating_themes.html • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/mautic/core/CVE-2026-9558/
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate administrator installing or updating a theme zip via Settings > Themes
  • Mautic version upgrade repopulating bundled themes (blank, cards, nature, etc.) into themes/
  • Marketing/design team uploading a custom corporate email/page theme
  • CI/CD or deployment automation syncing theme directories as the web user
  • Theme builder saving edits to email.html.twig / page.html.twig from the UI
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify which Mautic user triggered the write via the app audit log (Settings > Audit Log) and correlate the timestamp with the FolderPath; a new theme folder name you don't recognize, or a modified base/page/email .twig on an internet-facing host, is suspicious. Grab and read the .twig content for SSTI markers (_self.env, registerUndefinedFilterCallback, getFilter, system/exec/passthru/proc_open). 2) Contain: quarantine the theme file, revoke core:themes:create from the acting user pending review, and confirm the host is on a patched build (7.1.2/6.0.9/5.2.11/4.4.20). 3) Hunt: run UC1 on the same DeviceName for a php-spawned shell within minutes of the write, and review web/access logs for the theme-install POST and subsequent theme-preview/render requests.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has "/themes/" and FileName endswith ".twig"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "php" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath has "/themes/" and TargetFileName endswith ".twig"
| where ActingProcessName has "php" or ActingProcessName has_any ("httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Affected zebrad (<= v4.4.1) exposure to P2SH sigop consensus-split (CVE-2026-52735) AIExploitation High
Surfaces hosts with an installed Zebra/zebrad build at or below v4.4.1, which undercounts P2SH sigops and can be forced into a chain split from zcashd. This is asset-exposure hunting: identify vulnerable Zcash full nodes before an attacker broadcasts malicious P2SH-spend transactions. Rationale: Uses the concrete affected boundary from the advisory (zebrad <= v4.4.1, patched in 4.4.2) and CVE-2026-52735. parse_version gives an exact vulnerable-version test; SoftwareName 'zebrad' avoids collision with unrelated Zebra Technologies printer software. Note: GHSA-2prc-cj5x-4443 later found the 4.4.2 fix incomplete, so 4.5.1 is the true-safe floor. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-gf9r-m956-97qx • https://zfnd.org/zebra-4-5-1-security-fixes/ • https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-2prc-cj5x-4443 • https://dailycve.com/zebra-consensus-divergence-critical/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Zebra Technologies label-printer / barcode driver software matching the 'zebra' string (mitigated by SoftwareName 'zebrad' filter)
  • Decommissioned or lab-only Zcash test nodes that never touch mainnet consensus
  • Host already upgraded but vuln scanner holding a stale software-inventory record
  • Vulnerability scanner mis-mapping a different Zebra advisory to this CVE
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareVendor !has "Zebra Technologies" and SoftwareName !has "printer"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host actually runs a validating full node (not just an installed binary) and note the exact SoftwareVersion — anything < 4.4.2 is exposed to CVE-2026-52735. 2) Contain: schedule upgrade to a patched build; because the 4.4.2 fix was found incomplete (GHSA-2prc-cj5x-4443), upgrade straight to >= 4.5.1. Until patched, monitor the node's chain tip against a reference zcashd node for divergence. 3) Hunt: enumerate all zebrad hosts via inventory, and pivot to UC 'zebrad node process execution' and the 'bad-blk-sigops' log hunt to see whether an exploit block was already accepted.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareName has "zebrad" or (SoftwareVendor has "Zcash" and SoftwareName has "zebra")
| where isnotempty(SoftwareVersion)
| where parse_version(SoftwareVersion) < parse_version("4.4.2")   // 4.4.2 = first patched build per CVE-2026-52735

zebrad node process execution at vulnerable version (CVE-2026-52735) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts live execution of the zebrad binary and surfaces its product version so analysts can confirm exposure to the P2SH sigop-undercount consensus split. Complements inventory-based detection by catching nodes launched from non-packaged paths (source builds, containers) that TVM may miss. Rationale: Anchors on the exact binary name 'zebrad' from the advisory and surfaces ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion so analysts can read the version off Windows builds; Linux builds (no version info) are still surfaced rather than dropped. Distinct pivot from the TVM inventory UC — catches source/container launches inventory misses. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-gf9r-m956-97qx • https://zfnd.org/zebra-4-5-1-security-fixes/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate zebrad node operators running an already-patched build (>= 4.5.1) — version column disambiguates on Windows
  • CI/CD or automated test harnesses repeatedly spawning zebrad
  • Container orchestration restarting zebrad pods (high event volume, benign)
  • Linux hosts where product-version metadata is empty, forcing manual version confirmation
Suppression filter
| where isempty(ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion) or parse_version(ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion) < parse_version("4.4.2")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion; if empty (typical on Linux), query the node RPC/`zebrad --version` to get the build. Versions < 4.4.2 are exposed. 2) Contain: for exposed validating nodes, plan upgrade to >= 4.5.1 (the 4.4.2 patch was incomplete) and watch the chain tip vs a reference zcashd. 3) Hunt: for every host seen running zebrad, run the 'bad-blk-sigops' log-reject hunt and cross-check the inventory UC to build the full affected-asset list.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "zebrad" or FileName =~ "zebrad.exe"
| where isempty(ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion) or parse_version(ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion) < parse_version("4.4.2")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "zebrad"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, SHA256, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Google Disrupts NetNut Residential Proxy Network Spanning 2 Million Home Devices

The Hacker News
2026-07-02 7 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Google has significantly degraded NetNut, one of the biggest networks that turns home devices into rented relays for other people's traffic. Working with the FBI, Lumen, and others, Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG)&nbsp;said this week&nbsp;it had reduced the network's pool of usable devices by millions. Google identifies NetNut, also tracked as Popa, as a network spread across home

Domainsnetnut.com netnut.io

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Enterprise asset contacting NetNut/Popa residential-proxy gateway (netnut.com/netnut.io) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Enterprise asset contacting NetNut/Popa residential-proxy gateway (netnut.com/netnut.io) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts managed endpoints resolving or connecting to the NetNut (aka Popa) commercial proxy gateway domains named in the article. On a corporate asset this indicates either an embedded NetNut SDK/proxyware component phoning home (turning the host into a rented exit node) or an insider routing traffic through the seized residential-proxy service — neither of which is legitimate enterprise traffic. Rationale: Uses the two concrete IOC domains (netnut.com, netnut.io) named in the article as the only high-fidelity anchor; corroborated by Google Cloud GTIG blog and KrebsOnSecurity confirming NetNut=Popa and the SDK-based exit-node model, though neither disclosed C2 domains/package names, so the gateway domains are the sole reliable pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/google-continued-disruption-residential-proxy-networks/ • https://krebsonsecurity.com/2026/07/fbi-seizes-netnut-proxy-platform-popa-botnet/ • https://cybernews.com/news/google-fbi-disrupt-netnut-botnet-2-million-devices/
ATT&CKT1090.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or threat-intel analyst browsing netnut.com to read the FBI seizure notice
  • Marketing/ad-verification or QA team legitimately evaluating a residential-proxy service for geo-testing
  • Automated URL-detonation sandbox or web crawler visiting the domain from a lab subnet
  • SOC analyst pivoting on the IOC and clicking the domain during triage
  • Corporate DNS resolver forwarding a downstream user's one-off lookup
Suppression filter
and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","iexplore.exe","opera.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Identify the initiating process/host — is the connection browser-driven (likely a human visiting the site) or from a non-browser/service process (strong proxyware/SDK signal)? Check whether the host is a managed asset vs a lab/sandbox and whether contacts are repeated/beaconing vs a single lookup. 2) Contain: If a non-browser process is beaconing, isolate the host, block netnut.com/netnut.io and resolved IPs at the proxy/firewall, and quarantine the associated binary for analysis. 3) Hunt: Sweep the environment for the same process hash and for other known bandwidth-sharing/proxyware domains; review the host for unauthorized 'earn-money-for-bandwidth' apps and check whether it acted as an exit node (unexpected inbound/relayed connections) or was co-opted into Mirai/Badbox-style activity.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("netnut.com","netnut.io")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Connections=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,10), RemoteIPs=make_set(RemoteIP,10), SampleProc=any(InitiatingProcessFileName), SampleCmd=any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Connections desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("netnut.com","netnut.io")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Queries=count(), Responses=make_set(DnsResponseName,10) by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery
| order by Queries desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] The Gentlemen Go backdoor C2 beacon to 81.177.215.15:9443 · [LLM] Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared) deployment for persistent covert access · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. The Gentlemen Go backdoor C2 beacon to 81.177.215.15:9443 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the hardcoded command-and-control channel of The Gentlemen RaaS Go/Yamux backdoor, which opens a persistent bidirectional TCP session to 81.177.215.15 on port 9443 and executes operator commands via cmd.exe or opens a SOCKS proxy. The fixed IP+port pair makes this a high-fidelity network IOC. Rationale: Uses the exact C2 tuple 81.177.215.15:9443 confirmed by Kaspersky Securelist as The Gentlemen's Yamux Go backdoor endpoint — a fixed IP+port is one of the highest-fidelity network IOCs available. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/the-gentlemen-raas/120447/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ransomware-groups-turn-to-citrix-bleed.html
ATT&CKT1095 T1571 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/sandbox detonation host deliberately connecting to the IOC
  • Security researcher or IR team validating the indicator
  • Shared NAT egress where a single benign host and a compromised host both egress the same public IP (only affects source attribution, not the destination match)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating process on the connecting host (InitiatingProcessFileName/CommandLine) — a Go binary in %TEMP%/%ProgramData% or an unsigned exe strongly confirms the backdoor. Step 2 (contain): Network-isolate the host, block 81.177.215.15:9443 at the perimeter, and capture the implant binary before deletion (actors delete payloads post-exec). Step 3 (hunt): Sweep all hosts for connections to this IP, for cmd.exe children of the implant process, and for SOCKS-proxy listeners; pivot to PsExec/GPO lateral movement noted for The Gentlemen.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "81.177.215.15" and RemotePort == 9443
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "81.177.215.15" and DestinationPort == 9443
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName=SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceProduct, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: The Gentlemen Backdoor C2 Connection to 81.177.215.15:9443
id: 6f3a1c9e-2b47-4d8a-9c11-7e5b0a4d2f18
description: Detects outbound connection to The Gentlemen RaaS Go backdoor C2 endpoint
references:
  - https://securelist.com/the-gentlemen-raas/120447/
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ransomware-groups-turn-to-citrix-bleed.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/03
tags:
  - attack.command_and_control
  - attack.t1095
  - attack.t1571
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    DestinationIp: '81.177.215.15'
    DestinationPort: 9443
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationIp:81.177.215.15 @DestinationPort:9443
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4="81.177.215.15" RemotePort=9443
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest="81.177.215.15" All_Traffic.dest_port=9443 by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port, All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest="81.177.215.15" All_Traffic.dest_port=9443 by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port, All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Kontron ktapi.sys vulnerable driver load (The Gentlemen BYOVD) AIInstallation High
Hunts the load or install of the Kontron ktapi.sys kernel driver that The Gentlemen RaaS weaponised as a zero-day BYOVD to gain kernel R/W and terminate protected Microsoft, ESET, Palo Alto, and SentinelOne security processes. ktapi.sys has no legitimate enterprise footprint, so any load is suspicious. Rationale: ktapi.sys is the specific Kontron driver named in the article and corroborated by Expel as the zero-day BYOVD used to kill Microsoft/ESET/PAN/SentinelOne processes; the driver has effectively zero legitimate presence, making a bare name match high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://expel.com/blog/not-very-gentlemanly-analyzing-a-zero-day-exploit-used-by-the-gentlemen-ransomware-to-disable-targets-edrs/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ransomware-groups-turn-to-citrix-bleed.html
ATT&CKT1068 T1562.001 T1547.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Kontron industrial/embedded hardware where the vendor API is legitimately installed (rare outside OT/manufacturing)
  • Security researcher detonating the driver in a lab
  • AV/EDR quarantine engine copying the sample (InitiatingProcess would be the security product itself)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","CSFalconService.exe") // exclude EDR quarantine engines copying the sample
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the driver path and the process that wrote/loaded it; check whether the host is genuine Kontron OT hardware (if not, treat as malicious immediately). Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, verify EDR/AV agents are still running (BYOVD kills them), and add ktapi.sys to the Microsoft vulnerable-driver blocklist / WDAC policy. Step 3 (hunt): Look for security-process termination events, subsequent ransomware staging, and the same driver hash across the estate; correlate with The Gentlemen C2 (81.177.215.15) and PsExec/GPO lateral movement.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "ktapi.sys"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 7045
| where ServiceFileName has "ktapi.sys"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, InstalledBy=SubjectUserName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceType, ServiceStartType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_path, min(_time) as firstTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="ktapi.sys" by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.file_name, Filesystem.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`

Citrix Bleed 2 (CVE-2025-5777) exploitation attempts against NetScaler Gateway AIExploitation High
Detects exploitation of CitrixBleed 2 against NetScaler ADC/Gateway — the initial-access vector used by Anubis affiliates. Malformed POST requests to /p/u/doAuthentication.do that omit the passwd parameter and/or carry an oversized attacker-controlled User-Agent trigger the out-of-bounds memory read; high request volume from a single source indicates mass scanning. Rationale: Targets the exact CVE-2025-5777 exploit endpoint /p/u/doAuthentication.do with the documented malformed-POST + oversized-User-Agent signature (per Splunk, GreyNoise and watchTowr analyses), the initial-access method Arctic Wolf attributed to Anubis. Defender/Datadog/Falcon left empty — NetScaler HTTP telemetry is not shipped to endpoint EDR; this lives in appliance/WAF/proxy logs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.splunk.com/en_us/blog/security/citrixbleed-vulnerability-detection-mitigation.html • https://www.greynoise.io/blog/exploitation-citrixbleed-2-cve-2025-5777-before-public-poc • https://labs.watchtowr.com/how-much-more-must-we-bleed-citrix-netscaler-memory-disclosure-citrixbleed-2-cve-2025-5777/
ATT&CKT1190 T1212
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate high-volume authentication bursts from a corporate NAT egress (many users behind one IP)
  • Vulnerability scanners / authorised pentest tooling probing the endpoint
  • Load-balancer health checks hitting the auth endpoint
  • Mobile clients with unusually long but benign User-Agent strings
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm NetScaler build is unpatched for CVE-2025-5777; review the source IP reputation and whether the POSTs lack the passwd parameter or carry an abnormal UA. Step 2 (contain): If exploited, patch/upgrade NetScaler, terminate all active ICA/PCoIP and AAA sessions (kill leaked tokens), and block the source IPs. Step 3 (hunt): Look for post-auth session reuse from new geos/ASNs, follow-on RDP/SMB, PsExec service creation, and RMM tool deployment consistent with the Anubis playbook.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where DeviceVendor has "Citrix" or DeviceProduct has_any ("NetScaler","ADC","Gateway")
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/p/u/doAuthentication.do"
| extend UALen = strlen(RequestClientApplication)
| summarize Requests=count(), MaxUALen=max(UALen), SampleUA=any(RequestClientApplication), Hosts=dcount(DestinationHostName) by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where MaxUALen > 200 or Requests > 50   // oversized UA = leak payload; >50/hr = scanning
| order by Requests desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agents, values(Web.dest) as dest from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.http_method=POST Web.url="*/p/u/doAuthentication.do*" by Web.src, Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | eval ua_len=len(http_user_agent) | where ua_len>200 OR count>50 | sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agents, values(Web.dest) as dest from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.http_method=POST Web.url="*/p/u/doAuthentication.do*" by Web.src, Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | eval ua_len=len(http_user_agent) | where ua_len>200 OR count>50 | sort - count
Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared) deployment for persistent covert access AICommand & Control Medium
Detects Anubis affiliates configuring a Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared) to reach victim environments through an outbound-only encrypted channel that bypasses inbound firewall rules. Flags cloudflared execution with tunnel arguments or trycloudflare tokens, including renamed binaries invoking the tunnel subcommand. Rationale: Article explicitly states select Anubis intrusions 'configure a Cloudflare Tunnel (aka cloudflared)'; matches the cloudflared binary plus the tunnel/token/trycloudflare arguments so renamed binaries invoking the tunnel subcommand are still caught. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ransomware-groups-turn-to-citrix-bleed.html
ATT&CKT1572 T1090
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers legitimately using Cloudflare Tunnel to expose a local web app
  • IT teams using cloudflared for sanctioned remote access to internal services
  • CI/CD runners establishing ephemeral trycloudflare tunnels for previews
  • Sysadmins testing Cloudflare Zero Trust connectors
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("code.exe","node.exe") // exclude common developer parents when cloudflared is sanctioned
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Determine if cloudflared is sanctioned on the host; inspect the tunnel token/config and the parent process (RMM tool or cmd.exe parenting cloudflared is suspicious). Step 2 (contain): Kill the cloudflared process, isolate the host, and block Cloudflare tunnel FQDNs/egress if unauthorised. Step 3 (hunt): Look for co-located RMM tooling, PsExec service creation, credential access, and the Anubis exfil stack (rclone/s5cmd/WinSCP) on the same and adjacent hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "cloudflared.exe"
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("tunnel run","--token ","trycloudflare.com","cloudflared tunnel")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\cloudflared.exe"
   or CommandLine has_any ("tunnel run","--token ","trycloudflare.com","cloudflared tunnel")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account=SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Anubis defense impairment: Defender RTP disable + SophosUninstall + PCHunter AIInstallation High
Hunts the Anubis pre-encryption defense-evasion cluster: disabling Windows Defender real-time protection via Set-MpPreference/registry, running SophosUninstall, and dropping PCHunter (a kernel process/driver killer). Any one of these in user context is a strong hands-on-keyboard defense-impairment signal. Rationale: Directly encodes the three named Anubis defense-evasion artifacts from the article (Defender real-time protection disablement, SophosUninstall activity, PCHunter-related artifacts); machine accounts excluded to keep FPs low. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ransomware-groups-turn-to-citrix-bleed.html
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1089
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned Sophos removal during an approved EDR migration
  • IT/helpdesk temporarily disabling Defender RTP for a legit software install or troubleshooting
  • Sysadmin using PCHunter for benign rootkit troubleshooting
  • MDM/RMM tooling toggling Defender settings as part of policy management
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","intunemanagementextension.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "DisableRealtimeMonitoring") // exclude sanctioned MDM policy toggles
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Check for a change ticket authorising Defender/Sophos changes; review the initiating process and account — RMM or PsExec parentage plus off-hours timing escalates severity. Step 2 (contain): Re-enable Defender RTP, isolate the host, and preserve PCHunter/driver artifacts; verify no BYOVD driver (ktapi.sys) is loaded. Step 3 (hunt): Look for immediately following shadow-copy deletion, mass file encryption, and the /WIPEMODE encryptor across the estate; confirm which accounts triggered the changes and their lateral spread.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("PCHunter64.exe","PCHunter.exe","PCHunter32.exe")
   or FileName has "SophosUninstall"
   or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "Set-MpPreference" and ProcessCommandLine has "DisableRealtimeMonitoring")
   or ProcessCommandLine has "DisableRealtimeMonitoring $true"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("PCHunter64.exe","PCHunter.exe","PCHunter32.exe","SophosUninstall")
   or (NewProcessName has "powershell" and CommandLine has "Set-MpPreference" and CommandLine has "DisableRealtimeMonitoring")
   or CommandLine has "DisableRealtimeMonitoring $true"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account=SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Anubis Ransomware Defense Impairment Cluster

Anubis exfiltration tooling: rclone/s5cmd/S3 Browser/WinSCP cloud transfer AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the Anubis pre-ransomware data-transfer stack — rclone, s5cmd, S3 Browser, WinSCP, and PuTTY/pscp — used to stage and exfiltrate data to attacker-controlled cloud/SFTP storage. Matches the tool binaries plus cloud-copy verbs/remote arguments so renamed rclone/s5cmd builds are still caught. Rationale: Directly lists the exfil tools named in the article (S3 Browser, rclone, s5cmd, WinSCP, PuTTY/pscp) and pairs them with cloud-copy/remote arguments so renamed rclone/s5cmd binaries are still surfaced; kept as hunting tier because these tools have legitimate admin use. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ransomware-groups-turn-to-citrix-bleed.html
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1048
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup/DevOps teams using rclone or s5cmd for sanctioned S3 sync jobs
  • Admins using WinSCP/PuTTY for routine SFTP file management
  • Data engineers using S3 Browser for legitimate bucket work
  • Scheduled automation copying data to approved cloud storage
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","cloudberry.exe") and FileName in~ ("rclone.exe","s5cmd.exe")) // exclude sanctioned backup automation
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Check whether the tool is sanctioned for the host/user and inspect the remote target in the command line — attacker-controlled buckets/SFTP hosts confirm exfil. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, block the destination endpoints, and revoke any cloud credentials referenced in configs. Step 3 (hunt): Estimate data staged/transferred (volumes, archive creation), and look for the follow-on Anubis encryptor (/WIPEMODE), Defender disablement, and PsExec lateral movement.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("rclone.exe","s5cmd.exe","s3browser.exe","winscp.exe","winscp.com","pscp.exe")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("rclone ","s5cmd ")
| where FileName in~ ("s3browser.exe","winscp.exe","winscp.com")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("copy","sync","--config","remote:"," cp "," mb ","cat ")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("rclone.exe","s5cmd.exe","s3browser.exe","winscp.exe","winscp.com","pscp.exe")
   or CommandLine has_any ("rclone ","s5cmd ")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("s3browser.exe","winscp.exe") or CommandLine has_any ("copy","sync","--config","remote:"," cp ")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account=SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Anubis encryptor /WIPEMODE destructive command execution AIActions on Objectives High
Detects execution of the Anubis ransomware encryptor with its distinctive /WIPEMODE switch, which reduces victim files to 0 KB regardless of ransom payment. Also matches the Anubis flag combination (/KEY /PATH /elevated) used to invoke the encryptor with elevated privileges. Rationale: The /WIPEMODE switch is documented by Rubrik Zero Labs (cited in-article) as the Anubis wiper module that zeroes files to 0 KB — a unique, article-specific command-line token; the /KEY /PATH /elevated combo covers standard encryptor invocation. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ransomware-groups-turn-to-citrix-bleed.html
ATT&CKT1485 T1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate software using a coincidentally-named /WIPEMODE or /KEY switch (rare; validate the parent binary)
  • Security team detonating the Anubis sample in a sandbox
  • Red-team ransomware simulation exercise
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): This is near-certainly malicious — confirm the executing binary/hash and whether /WIPEMODE was reached (data destruction imminent/underway). Step 2 (contain): Immediately isolate the host from network and storage, kill the process, and trigger the ransomware IR playbook; protect backups/shadow copies from deletion. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep for the same binary hash and command line across all hosts, block lateral movement (PsExec/RDP/SMB), and verify no other systems have staged the encryptor; assess whether /WIPEMODE has already zeroed files for recovery planning.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/WIPEMODE"
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "/KEY" and ProcessCommandLine has "/PATH" and ProcessCommandLine has "/elevated")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "/WIPEMODE"
   or (CommandLine has "/KEY" and CommandLine has "/PATH" and CommandLine has "/elevated")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account=SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent

| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-5777")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-5777")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2025-5777")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2025-5777")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
