     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("api.service.bio")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("api.service.bio")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("api.service.bio")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'

falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"

      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

| where files > 200

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ToddyCat-Linked Umbrij Malware Abuses OAuth to Access Gmail via Google API

The Hacker News
2026-07-02 17 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The threat actor known as ToddyCat has been attributed to a new malware called Umbrij that's designed to gain surreptitious access to a victim's email correspondence via the Google API. "In this campaign, the attackers focused their attention on corporate email communications hosted on Gmail, targeting access compromise via APIs," Kaspersky said in a detailed report published this week. "

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Umbrij DLL side-load via BDSubWiz / VSTestVideoRecorder / GoogleDesktop signed hosts · [LLM] Scheduled task masquerading as Kaspersky EDR (KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp) · [LLM] Umbrij (ToddyCat) known-bad hash match on endpoint · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Google OAuth endpoint callout from browser spawned by Umbrij side-load host

Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Browser profile artifacts copied into Chrome/Edge 'BackupFiles' staging directory · [LLM] Headless Chromium launched with remote-debugging-port on copied BackupFiles profile (STRD) · [LLM] Grant/use of 'Google Workspace Migration for Microsoft Outlook' OAuth app (Umbrij impersonation) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Umbrij DLL side-load via BDSubWiz / VSTestVideoRecorder / GoogleDesktop signed hosts AIInstallation High
Hunts ToddyCat's Umbrij deployment where three legitimately-signed but out-of-place binaries (Bitdefender BDSubWiz.exe, Visual Studio VSTestVideoRecorder.exe, discontinued GoogleDesktop.exe) side-load the attacker's hijacking DLL (log.dll / Microsoft.VisualStudio.QualityTools.VideoRecorderEngine.dll / GoogleServices.dll). Article-specific because it pairs the exact host binary with its exact hijackable DLL name from outside its legitimate install path. Rationale: Uses the exact host-binary + hijackable-DLL pairs disclosed by Securelist (BDSubWiz.exe->log.dll, VSTestVideoRecorder.exe->VideoRecorderEngine.dll, GoogleDesktop.exe->GoogleServices.dll); requiring the pairing plus a non-Program-Files path makes this near-zero FP. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://gbhackers.com/toddycat-uses-shadow-token/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/toddycat-linked-umbrij-malware-abuses.html
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Bitdefender ConnectAgent submission wizard running from its real Program Files path (excluded by path filter)
  • Visual Studio automated UI/test recording on a developer workstation from the VS install directory
  • Portable/relocated copy of a legit Google Desktop install by a nostalgic user
  • Security tooling or EDR replaying/quarantining the binary from a sandbox path
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host binary and loaded DLL folder path — legitimate copies live under Program Files; anything under %TEMP%, %APPDATA%, ProgramData or a user-writable dir is malicious. Pull the DLL SHA256/MD5 and compare to the Umbrij hash list. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the host process, and quarantine both the signed EXE and the side-loaded DLL; disable the account whose token was likely duplicated. 3) Hunt: check for a scheduled task named 'KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp', for a '\BackupFiles\' folder under the Chrome/Edge profile, and for headless browser launches with --remote-debugging-port on the same host.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "BDSubWiz.exe" and FileName =~ "log.dll")
     or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "VSTestVideoRecorder.exe" and FileName =~ "Microsoft.VisualStudio.QualityTools.VideoRecorderEngine.dll")
     or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "GoogleDesktop.exe" and FileName =~ "GoogleServices.dll")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, LoadedDll = FileName, DllPath = FolderPath, SHA256, MD5
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("BDSubWiz.exe","VSTestVideoRecorder.exe","GoogleDesktop.exe")
| where NewProcessName !startswith "C:\\Program Files"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Scheduled task masquerading as Kaspersky EDR (KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp) AIInstallation High
Detects creation of a scheduled task impersonating Kaspersky's endpoint product ('KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp') that ToddyCat used to launch the signed DLL side-load host for Umbrij. Article-specific because the exact fake task name is the persistence/execution trigger Kaspersky observed during threat hunting. Rationale: The literal task name 'KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp' is a direct IOC from Kaspersky's report; genuine Kaspersky products do not create a task under this exact string, so a match is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/toddycat-linked-umbrij-malware-abuses.html
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine Kaspersky deployment tool that happens to embed the product name in a task (verify signer and target binary)
  • Internal software-inventory or naming audit tooling that references the string in a task description
  • Red-team/purple-team emulation of this ToddyCat TTP
  • EDR/backup agents creating similarly named housekeeping tasks (check the launched image path)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "Kaspersky Lab"
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the task action/XML — a benign Kaspersky task points at avp.exe under Program Files\Kaspersky Lab; a malicious one launches BDSubWiz.exe/VSTestVideoRecorder.exe/GoogleDesktop.exe from a user-writable path. 2) Contain: delete the rogue task, isolate the host, and quarantine the launched EXE+DLL. 3) Hunt: pivot on the launched binary for the corresponding side-load image-load event and for BackupFiles browser-profile staging on the same device.

| where ActionType == "ScheduledTaskCreated"
| where AdditionalFields has "KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc

| where EventID == 4698
| where EventData has "KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, SubjectDomainName, EventData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Browser profile artifacts copied into Chrome/Edge 'BackupFiles' staging directory AIActions on Objectives High
Detects Umbrij staging stolen browser data: creation of Login Data / Web Data / Preferences / Secure Preferences and related files inside a 'BackupFiles' directory under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Google\Chrome or %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Edge. Article-specific because the exact staging folder name and copied artifact set are unique to Umbrij's workflow. Rationale: The 'BackupFiles' folder name plus the exact copied artifact set (Login Data, Web Data, Secure Preferences, Login Data For Account) under the Chrome/Edge profile is a unique Umbrij fingerprint; excluding the browser itself as writer removes benign profile writes. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://gbhackers.com/toddycat-uses-shadow-token/

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • IT profile-migration scripts moving Login Data during a machine refresh
  • Browser sync/repair tooling copying Secure Preferences
  • Security researcher manually cloning a profile for analysis
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","explorer.exe","setup.exe","msiexec.exe")

1) Triage: identify the writing process (InitiatingProcessFileName) — if it is a signed side-load host (BDSubWiz/VSTest/GoogleDesktop) or an unknown .NET binary, treat as confirmed. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the writer, delete the BackupFiles directory, and force-revoke browser/Google sessions for the profile's user. 3) Hunt: look for a subsequent headless browser launch with --remote-debugging-port using the BackupFiles path and for outbound OAuth calls to accounts.google.com from that host.

Headless Chromium launched with remote-debugging-port on copied BackupFiles profile (STRD) AIActions on Objectives High
Core of ToddyCat's Shadow Token via Remote Debug (STRD) technique: chrome.exe/msedge.exe started in headless mode with a remote debugging port, pointed at the copied 'BackupFiles' profile so all live cookies/sessions apply and Puppeteer can drive the Gmail OAuth flow. Article-specific via the combination of remote-debugging-port + BackupFiles user-data-dir. Rationale: Combines the Umbrij-specific '--remote-debugging-port' automation flag with a '--user-data-dir' pointing at the copied 'BackupFiles' profile; legitimate remote-debug usage almost never targets a cloned BackupFiles directory, giving very low FP. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://gbhackers.com/toddycat-uses-shadow-token/
ATT&CKT1539 T1528 T1185
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Front-end developers or QA automation using Puppeteer/Playwright with --remote-debugging-port (but not against a BackupFiles profile)
  • Automated screenshot/PDF rendering pipelines launching headless Chrome
  • Browser automation for synthetic monitoring
  • Security testing frameworks driving Chromium via CDP
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has "BackupFiles" and (ProcessCommandLine has @"\Google\Chrome\" or ProcessCommandLine has @"\Microsoft\Edge\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: examine the full command line — the presence of a --user-data-dir under a '\BackupFiles\' path derived from the user's profile confirms Umbrij; note the parent process. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate the headless browser and its parent, kill the debug port session, and revoke the user's Google/Gmail sessions and OAuth grants immediately. 3) Hunt: check %MYACCOUNT%/connections-equivalent audit for a new 'Google Workspace Migration/Sync for Microsoft Outlook' grant and inspect Umbrij's log file for a captured authorization code before exfiltration.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "BackupFiles"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "BackupFiles"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Google OAuth endpoint callout from browser spawned by Umbrij side-load host AICommand & Control High
Detects the STRD OAuth request phase: a Chromium browser whose parent is one of the Umbrij side-load hosts (BDSubWiz/VSTestVideoRecorder/GoogleDesktop) reaching accounts.google.com/o/oauth2 or oauth2.googleapis.com. Article-specific because it ties the Google OAuth callout to the exact malicious parent-process chain rather than flagging generic Gmail traffic. Rationale: Pivots on InitiatingProcessParentFileName being an Umbrij side-load host while the browser reaches the exact Google OAuth hosts; the parent-chain constraint is what makes it high-fidelity, and only Defender DeviceNetworkEvents reliably carries the browser's parent process. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/toddycat-linked-umbrij-malware-abuses.html

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Red-team emulation of the STRD chain
  • Analyst detonation of the sample in a monitored VM
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent side-load host and the OAuth URL; capture the browser command line (should show remote-debugging-port + BackupFiles). 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the process tree, and revoke the affected Google account's tokens and app grants. 3) Hunt: correlate to the same host's DLL side-load, scheduled task, and BackupFiles staging events to scope the full Umbrij deployment; check for exfiltration of the Umbrij log file containing the OAuth authorization code.

Grant/use of 'Google Workspace Migration for Microsoft Outlook' OAuth app (Umbrij impersonation) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the OAuth abuse endpoint of the campaign: an OAuth grant or Gmail/Drive access via the 'Google Workspace Migration for Microsoft Outlook' or 'Google Workspace Sync for Microsoft Outlook' application, whose client_id Umbrij impersonates to obtain full Gmail/Drive/Contacts/Calendar/Tasks scope. Requires Google Workspace activity surfaced through Defender for Cloud Apps. Rationale: Kaspersky's mitigation explicitly names the two migration/sync apps whose client_id Umbrij impersonates; matching those exact app names in Google Workspace OAuth activity flags accounts touched by the STRD token, though it needs a Workspace connector into MDCA. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/toddycat-linked-umbrij-malware-abuses.html
ATT&CKT1528 T1550.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Organizations legitimately migrating mailboxes from on-prem Exchange/Outlook to Google Workspace using the real GWMMO/GWSMO tools
  • A one-time authorized data-import project by IT
  • A user who genuinely installed Google Workspace Sync for Outlook
  • MSP-driven tenant migration activity
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm with IT whether any sanctioned Exchange->Workspace migration is in flight; if not, the grant is illicit. Note the granting user, source IP/geo and user-agent. 2) Contain: revoke the app's access at myaccount.google.com/connections for affected users to invalidate the OAuth tokens, force session reset and MFA re-enrollment. 3) Hunt: pivot each affected user back to endpoint telemetry for Umbrij side-loading, BackupFiles staging, and headless remote-debug browser launches; review Gmail/Drive audit logs for bulk message/file reads under the app.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application has "Google"
| where ObjectName has_any ("Google Workspace Migration for Microsoft Outlook","Google Workspace Sync for Microsoft Outlook")
     or ActivityObjects has_any ("Google Workspace Migration for Microsoft Outlook","Google Workspace Sync for Microsoft Outlook")
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, Application, ActionType, ActivityType, ObjectName, IPAddress, ISP, CountryCode, UserAgent
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
CloudAppEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Application has "Google"
| where ObjectName has_any ("Google Workspace Migration for Microsoft Outlook","Google Workspace Sync for Microsoft Outlook")
     or ActivityObjects has_any ("Google Workspace Migration for Microsoft Outlook","Google Workspace Sync for Microsoft Outlook")
| project TimeGenerated, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, Application, ActionType, ActivityType, ObjectName, IPAddress, ISP, CountryCode, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
Umbrij (ToddyCat) known-bad hash match on endpoint AIInstallation Medium
Direct IOC alerting on the ten MD5 hashes attributed to Umbrij by Kaspersky, matched against image loads, file writes and process executions. Catches the malware regardless of which side-load host or command-line variant delivers it. Rationale: Ships the ten Umbrij MD5s from the Kaspersky/Securelist report across image-load, file-write and process telemetry; because Umbrij is a side-loaded .NET DLL, the image-load and file-write arms matter as much as process execution. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/toddycat-linked-umbrij-malware-abuses.html
ATT&CKT1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hash collision is negligible for MD5-of-a-specific-file at this scale, so FPs are effectively limited to an analyst intentionally staging the sample
  • Threat-intel/EDR product reprocessing the file in a sandbox
  • AV quarantine copies of the same file being re-scanned
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the hit is a live on-disk/loaded file (not a quarantined copy) and capture the host, user and full path. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the artifact, and treat the associated user's Google/Gmail sessions and OAuth grants as compromised — revoke them. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same hashes and for the surrounding TTPs (side-load hosts, KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp task, BackupFiles staging, headless remote-debug); rotate credentials for any account whose profile was staged.
let UmbrijMD5 = dynamic(["1ab58838e5790efb22f2d35ab98c0b7d","a7d7d6c4c3f227f7117261c63b9e23a9","3d3a621f852c42d97fd7260681e42508","3432dd9ac0df80ef86eb80bd080f839b","22aaeb4946ba6d2f2e27feb7dbb295de","f61fbfb7aa1cd5dc8f70b055b51563e2","f169d6d172dfb775895a5e2b1540c854","9f5f2f0fb0a7f5aa9f16b9a7b6dad89f","28cb7b261f4eb97e8a4b3b0d32f8def1","bae82a15d1dbfb024617b9b56a8e5f66"]);
union
  (DeviceImageLoadEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where MD5 in~ (UmbrijMD5) | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Kind="ImageLoad", FileName, FolderPath, MD5, InitiatingProcessFileName),
  (DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where MD5 in~ (UmbrijMD5) | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Kind="FileWrite", FileName, FolderPath, MD5, InitiatingProcessFileName),
  (DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where MD5 in~ (UmbrijMD5) | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Kind="Process", FileName, FolderPath, MD5, InitiatingProcessFileName)
| order by Timestamp desc
let UmbrijMD5 = dynamic(["1ab58838e5790efb22f2d35ab98c0b7d","a7d7d6c4c3f227f7117261c63b9e23a9","3d3a621f852c42d97fd7260681e42508","3432dd9ac0df80ef86eb80bd080f839b","22aaeb4946ba6d2f2e27feb7dbb295de","f61fbfb7aa1cd5dc8f70b055b51563e2","f169d6d172dfb775895a5e2b1540c854","9f5f2f0fb0a7f5aa9f16b9a7b6dad89f","28cb7b261f4eb97e8a4b3b0d32f8def1","bae82a15d1dbfb024617b9b56a8e5f66"]);
union
  (ImProcessCreate | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where MD5 in~ (UmbrijMD5) | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, Kind="Process", TargetProcessName, MD5),
  (ImFileEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where TargetFileMD5 in~ (UmbrijMD5) | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, Kind="File", TargetFileName, MD5=TargetFileMD5)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId
RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard Installation High
ConnectWise / AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installed outside IT change windows = common tradecraft for ransomware affiliates and IT-helpdesk impersonators.
ATT&CKT1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe")
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\atera_agent.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\SplashtopStreamer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\RustDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1ab58838e5790efb22f2d35ab98c0b7d", "a7d7d6c4c3f227f7117261c63b9e23a9", "3d3a621f852c42d97fd7260681e42508", "3432dd9ac0df80ef86eb80bd080f839b", "22aaeb4946ba6d2f2e27feb7dbb295de", "f61fbfb7aa1cd5dc8f70b055b51563e2", "f169d6d172dfb775895a5e2b1540c854", "9f5f2f0fb0a7f5aa9f16b9a7b6dad89f", "28cb7b261f4eb97e8a4b3b0d32f8def1", "bae82a15d1dbfb024617b9b56a8e5f66") or SHA1 in~ ("1ab58838e5790efb22f2d35ab98c0b7d", "a7d7d6c4c3f227f7117261c63b9e23a9", "3d3a621f852c42d97fd7260681e42508", "3432dd9ac0df80ef86eb80bd080f839b", "22aaeb4946ba6d2f2e27feb7dbb295de", "f61fbfb7aa1cd5dc8f70b055b51563e2", "f169d6d172dfb775895a5e2b1540c854", "9f5f2f0fb0a7f5aa9f16b9a7b6dad89f", "28cb7b261f4eb97e8a4b3b0d32f8def1", "bae82a15d1dbfb024617b9b56a8e5f66") or MD5 in~ ("1ab58838e5790efb22f2d35ab98c0b7d", "a7d7d6c4c3f227f7117261c63b9e23a9", "3d3a621f852c42d97fd7260681e42508", "3432dd9ac0df80ef86eb80bd080f839b", "22aaeb4946ba6d2f2e27feb7dbb295de", "f61fbfb7aa1cd5dc8f70b055b51563e2", "f169d6d172dfb775895a5e2b1540c854", "9f5f2f0fb0a7f5aa9f16b9a7b6dad89f", "28cb7b261f4eb97e8a4b3b0d32f8def1", "bae82a15d1dbfb024617b9b56a8e5f66")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1ab58838e5790efb22f2d35ab98c0b7d", "a7d7d6c4c3f227f7117261c63b9e23a9", "3d3a621f852c42d97fd7260681e42508", "3432dd9ac0df80ef86eb80bd080f839b", "22aaeb4946ba6d2f2e27feb7dbb295de", "f61fbfb7aa1cd5dc8f70b055b51563e2", "f169d6d172dfb775895a5e2b1540c854", "9f5f2f0fb0a7f5aa9f16b9a7b6dad89f", "28cb7b261f4eb97e8a4b3b0d32f8def1", "bae82a15d1dbfb024617b9b56a8e5f66") or SHA1 in~ ("1ab58838e5790efb22f2d35ab98c0b7d", "a7d7d6c4c3f227f7117261c63b9e23a9", "3d3a621f852c42d97fd7260681e42508", "3432dd9ac0df80ef86eb80bd080f839b", "22aaeb4946ba6d2f2e27feb7dbb295de", "f61fbfb7aa1cd5dc8f70b055b51563e2", "f169d6d172dfb775895a5e2b1540c854", "9f5f2f0fb0a7f5aa9f16b9a7b6dad89f", "28cb7b261f4eb97e8a4b3b0d32f8def1", "bae82a15d1dbfb024617b9b56a8e5f66") or MD5 in~ ("1ab58838e5790efb22f2d35ab98c0b7d", "a7d7d6c4c3f227f7117261c63b9e23a9", "3d3a621f852c42d97fd7260681e42508", "3432dd9ac0df80ef86eb80bd080f839b", "22aaeb4946ba6d2f2e27feb7dbb295de", "f61fbfb7aa1cd5dc8f70b055b51563e2", "f169d6d172dfb775895a5e2b1540c854", "9f5f2f0fb0a7f5aa9f16b9a7b6dad89f", "28cb7b261f4eb97e8a4b3b0d32f8def1", "bae82a15d1dbfb024617b9b56a8e5f66")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["1ab58838e5790efb22f2d35ab98c0b7d", "a7d7d6c4c3f227f7117261c63b9e23a9", "3d3a621f852c42d97fd7260681e42508", "3432dd9ac0df80ef86eb80bd080f839b", "22aaeb4946ba6d2f2e27feb7dbb295de", "f61fbfb7aa1cd5dc8f70b055b51563e2", "f169d6d172dfb775895a5e2b1540c854", "9f5f2f0fb0a7f5aa9f16b9a7b6dad89f", "28cb7b261f4eb97e8a4b3b0d32f8def1", "bae82a15d1dbfb024617b9b56a8e5f66"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: File or Process Matching Article Hash IOCs
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0b
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__HASH_LIST__` placeholder with article-specific SHA256

Its Threat Research Team calls the operator JADEPUFFER and says a large language model handled the whole job: breaking in, stealing credentials, moving deeper into the network, then encrypting and wiping a company's production database. Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).

Exploitation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Cron/systemd persistence beaconing to JADEPUFFER C2 45.131.66.106 · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] JADEPUFFER C2 beacon to 45.131.66.106:4444/beacon · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Database ransomware impact: README_RANSOM table / ransom-note strings + mass DROP · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Langflow unauthenticated RCE (CVE-2025-3248) via /api/v1/validate/code POST AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound POST requests to the Langflow code-validation endpoint that CVE-2025-3248 abuses for unauthenticated Python execution, the exact entry vector JADEPUFFER used. Article-specific because it pins the named CVE's documented vulnerable endpoint on an internet-facing Langflow box rather than a generic web exploit. Rationale: Pins CVE-2025-3248's documented vulnerable endpoint (/api/v1/validate/code) + POST, the exact unauthenticated-RCE path the article names as JADEPUFFER's way in. Defender left empty because MDE does not ingest reverse-proxy/web access logs; endpoint manifestation is covered by the execution UC. WebSearch was blocked in this session so no external corroboration could be pulled.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.006
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Langflow flow authors saving/validating custom Python components
  • Internal CI/CD or health-check jobs POSTing to the validate endpoint
  • Security scanners / ASM tools probing the known CVE path
  • Blue-team CVE-2025-3248 validation testing
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has "HealthCheck" and SourceIP !in ("127.0.0.1")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the request body/user-agent and source IP; confirm whether the payload contains exec/import/os/subprocess and whether the Langflow build is <1.3.0 (still vulnerable). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, take the Langflow instance off the public internet, and rotate every API key/cloud credential reachable from its environment. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for a child shell/interpreter spawned by uvicorn/gunicorn/python, beacons to 45.131.66.106, and new cron persistence.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/api/v1/validate/code"   // CVE-2025-3248 Langflow code-exec endpoint
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceProduct, DeviceVendor
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow web service (uvicorn/gunicorn/python) spawning shell or download tool AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the on-host manifestation of the Langflow RCE: the web-service process spawning a shell, curl, or wget to run recon and sweep secrets (MinIO minioadmin default, cloud keys) and reach the staging server 64.20.53.230. Article-specific because a Langflow/uvicorn parent spawning /bin/sh is the RCE payload firing, not normal app behaviour. Rationale: A public-facing Langflow/uvicorn process spawning /bin/sh or curl is the RCE detonating; enriched with the article's concrete secret-sweep artifacts (minioadmin default cred, staging IP 64.20.53.230, cloud-provider key names). WebSearch blocked so no second-source confirmation; grounded in article body.
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1059.004 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langflow custom components that legitimately shell out to system tools
  • In-container entrypoint scripts where python/uvicorn launches a shell at startup
  • Ops using curl/wget from an app-service context for package or model downloads
  • Health-check or exporter sidecars spawning shell probes
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("entrypoint.sh","docker-entrypoint") and FileName in~ ("sh","bash"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child command line for recon (id, uname, env), credential paths (.aws/credentials, minioadmin), or egress to 64.20.53.230. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the Langflow process tree, and rotate all secrets that lived in that environment (OpenAI/Anthropic/DeepSeek/Gemini keys, AWS/Azure/GCP/Alibaba/Tencent creds). 3) Hunt: pivot to network events for 45.131.66.106 and 64.20.53.230, and check for a new cron job beaconing every 30 minutes.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("uvicorn","gunicorn","python","python3","langflow","node")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| extend SecretSweep = ProcessCommandLine has_any ("minioadmin","64.20.53.230","credentials",".aws","OPENAI","ANTHROPIC","DEEPSEEK")
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("uvicorn","gunicorn","python","python3","langflow","node")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget")
| extend SecretSweep = ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("minioadmin","64.20.53.230","credentials",".aws")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SecretSweep
| order by TimeGenerated desc

JADEPUFFER C2 beacon to 45.131.66.106:4444/beacon AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any connection to the JADEPUFFER command-and-control IP 45.131.66.106, the target of a /beacon check-in on port 4444 every 30 minutes. Article-specific: a dedicated, published malicious IP + port + URI from Sysdig's IOC list. Rationale: 45.131.66.106 is Sysdig's published JADEPUFFER C2 IP with a documented :4444/beacon check-in every 30 minutes; a dedicated malicious IP makes any hit high-fidelity. WebSearch was blocked so the IOC is taken directly from the article's Sysdig indicator list without independent second-source confirmation.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/sandbox detonation infrastructure deliberately touching the IOC
  • Blue-team IOC-validation connectivity tests
  • A benign service that later gets assigned the same recycled VPS IP (verify timeframe)
  • Security scanner sweeping the /24 that includes this IP
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process/context making the connection (ContextImageFileName / InitiatingProcessFileName) and whether check-ins recur near a 30-minute cadence. 2) Contain: block 45.131.66.106 (and staging 64.20.53.230) egress at perimeter, isolate the beaconing host. 3) Hunt: on that host enumerate cron/systemd timers, look for the Langflow RCE parent-child chain, and check MySQL/Nacos hosts for README_RANSOM tables and dropped databases.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "45.131.66.106"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "45.131.66.106"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cron/systemd persistence beaconing to JADEPUFFER C2 45.131.66.106 AIInstallation High
Hunts the persistence mechanism: a scheduled job (cron/crond/atd) launching curl/wget/shell that contacts 45.131.66.106, the article's 'scheduled task that pinged the attacker's server every 30 minutes.' Distinct from the raw network IOC because it pivots on the scheduler parent, catching the persistence even if the beacon lands intermittently. Rationale: Combines the article's 30-minute scheduled-task persistence with the concrete C2 IP 45.131.66.106, pivoting on the cron parent so the persistence is caught even between beacon hits. WebSearch blocked; IOC and behaviour taken from the article/Sysdig indicators only.
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned monitoring cron jobs that curl an external endpoint (verify the IP)
  • Admin-authored heartbeat scripts to a legitimate host that shares the /24
  • Backup/telemetry agents scheduled via cron reaching out on interval
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the cron entry (crontab -l, /etc/cron.d/*, /var/spool/cron) and confirm the target IP and 30-minute cadence. 2) Contain: remove the malicious cron/systemd unit, block 45.131.66.106 egress, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: correlate to the Langflow RCE process chain and to any MySQL/Nacos host showing README_RANSOM or dropped tables; check for a MinIO server still on minioadmin default creds.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cron","crond","atd")
| where FileName in~ ("curl","wget","sh","bash","python","python3")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "45.131.66.106"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("cron","crond","atd")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("curl","wget","sh","bash")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "45.131.66.106"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Nacos auth bypass (CVE-2021-29441) via 'User-Agent: Nacos-Server' to create rogue admin AIExploitation High
Hunts requests to Nacos user-management endpoints carrying the User-Agent 'Nacos-Server' identity that CVE-2021-29441 abuses to bypass authentication and add an admin account, exactly what JADEPUFFER did before encrypting the config store. Article-specific: named CVE + Nacos default-signing-key takeover leading to a planted admin. Rationale: Uses CVE-2021-29441's well-known bypass signature — the spoofed 'Nacos-Server' User-Agent hitting /nacos/v1/auth/users to add an admin — which the article names as JADEPUFFER's Nacos takeover step. Defender/Falcon/Datadog empty because this is a web-request artifact those EDR/FDR feeds don't carry. WebSearch was blocked, so no external corroboration was obtained.
ATT&CKT1190 T1136.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Nacos cluster nodes using the Nacos-Server identity for inter-node calls (baseline internal peer IPs)
  • Security testing of the Nacos CVE by the blue team
  • Misconfigured client library that copies the Nacos-Server user-agent
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !startswith "10." and SourceIP !startswith "192.168."
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP is external/non-cluster and check whether a new Nacos user/admin was created around that time. 2) Contain: take Nacos off the public internet, rotate the default signing key, remove rogue admin accounts, and stop it connecting to its DB as root. 3) Hunt: check the backing MySQL for a README_RANSOM table and dropped tables, and correlate with the Langflow RCE host and C2 45.131.66.106.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestClientApplication has "Nacos-Server"   // CVE-2021-29441 identity-bypass User-Agent
| where RequestURL has "/nacos/v1/auth/users"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Database ransomware impact: README_RANSOM table / ransom-note strings + mass DROP AIActions on Objectives High
Alerts on JADEPUFFER's impact stage — creation of the README_RANSOM ransom table, presence of the ransom Bitcoin address / Proton contact, or a root-context mysql client issuing DROP TABLE/DROP DATABASE after the Nacos config store was encrypted. Article-specific via three unique published strings. Rationale: Three unique published IOCs — ransom table README_RANSOM, Bitcoin address 3J98t1WpEZ73CNmQviecrnyiWrnqRhWNLy, contact e78393397@proton.me — plus root-context mysql DROP make this near-zero-FP and specific to the JADEPUFFER impact stage. WebSearch was blocked so these strings are taken from the article's Sysdig indicator list without a second source.
ATT&CKT1486 T1485
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DBA restoring/testing on a lab copy who names a table README_RANSOM while investigating the IOC
  • Threat-hunt queries themselves logging the IOC strings into command lines
  • Legitimate scheduled DROP TABLE cleanup jobs (verify not root-from-internet and no ransom strings)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "threat-hunt" and AccountName != "dba-restore-svc"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the README_RANSOM table / note and whether DROP/TRUNCATE ran under the DB root account; identify the source session and host. 2) Contain: isolate the DB server, revoke internet exposure of the DB admin account, and preserve logs — note the actor claims AES but printed the key once and never saved it, so recovery from backups is the only path. 3) Hunt: trace back to the Nacos auth-bypass and Langflow RCE hosts, block C2 45.131.66.106 and staging 64.20.53.230, and audit MinIO for the minioadmin default login.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("README_RANSOM","3J98t1WpEZ73CNmQviecrnyiWrnqRhWNLy","e78393397@proton.me")
    or (FileName in~ ("mysql","mysqladmin") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("DROP TABLE","DROP DATABASE","TRUNCATE"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("README_RANSOM","3J98t1WpEZ73CNmQviecrnyiWrnqRhWNLy","e78393397@proton.me")
    or (SyslogMessage has_all ("DROP","TABLE") and SyslogMessage has "root")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: JADEPUFFER Database Ransomware Impact Strings

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-3248", "CVE-2021-29441")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-3248", "CVE-2021-29441")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
